rv: "Japoteurs" is a difficult animated short to review. On the one hand, the technical skill demonstrated by the animators is nothing short of astounding. The transition between the Japanese agent burning a hole in the newspaper and the hanger that houses the giant bomber is truly a classic. Yet, there is a combination of blanant racism, hightened and openly sanctioned by the war, and moments of "plot convinence playhouse." The Japanese "agent" is nearly silent, thus we never find out exactly who and where he comes from. His exaggerated features and style of speech are sadly typical of the portra

The Fleischer Superman cartoons were justly renowned for their high quality of animation. The stories were rather simple: Bad guy threatens evil (usually with Lois Lane in danger) and Superman saves the day. This is nothing different, but, as usual, the execution is first-rate. By the standards of the times, the film wasn't racist at all, of course, and there's little actual racism by today's standards. Spies are trying to steal the plane, but there's no ridicule and they are not racial charactures. They are spies.

Being that this was created in the U.S during the second world war, it's not surprising that a Japanese fellow would be cast as a bad guy. This was the enemy of democracy and freedom and that is Supe's main gig. I thought the portrayal of the enemy agent was quite subdued and done with the proper respect for such a hated and dreaded foe. They did after all let him hijack the plane and it took a Super-Man to foil his plans! I am always impressed with the stylized artwork and the detail of these old cartoons(note the windows of the elevator and the sheet metal of the aircraft. It's too bad they

Very likely this was meant to be spliced into the program on Friday February 12, 1932 (Lincoln's Birthday). I imagine this was made by some animation / title production company for distributors to offer as a bonus to theater owners or sold in a package with other topical short snippets to pepper into the program occasionally. I can see how movie houses might use this kind of thing to ingratiate themselves with their patrons and create a familial atmosphere that would make folks feel at home. Come on back now, ya' hear?

rv: That's an Actor, Not Edward R. Murrow

That's an actor portraying "Ed," (the only thing that Pete calls him during the broadcast.) That is not Edward R. Murrow. Seems to be a good, even-handed way of promoting a new show. I liked it myself.

This brief preview was never shown on CBS; it was produced for "PETE AND GLADYS"' primary sponsor, Carnation, so that the company could introduce their new program to their various executives and distributors at a special meeting, just before the series began in September 1960. Alan Dexter indeed portrays a fictional version of "Edward R. Murrow" here {the real Murrow would NEVER participate in this kind of promotion; besides, his "PERSON TO PERSON" series was being hosted by Charles Collingwood at the time, as Murrow had taken a year's sabbatical in Europe. When he returned in 1960, he was vi

The actors were good and they had pretty good scripts. I have no proble with Mr. Murrow doing this promo. Walter Cronkite appeared on Mary Tyler Moore, and several newscasters appeared on Murphy Brown. Senator John Glenn even appeared on Frazier. This did not degrade thme. They are all just human beings and I think they did it for a hoot. WHo cares, anyway?????

"Pete and Gladys", By all accounts, was hardly a great show, and indeed, it only ran for 2 seasons, never making the top 25. Still, as seen in this long promo, It was an decent enough TV series, featuring a good cast, and decent writing. Still, What makes this worth watching is it's insight into how the major TV networks promoted TV shows back then. With no internet, they created "promo reels".

Here's Ed Murrow, the Patron Saint of Broadcast Journalism, reduced to shilling for his own network and, indirectly, a milk company. With a laugh track, no less. The man who defeated Joe McCarthy couldn't defeat the CBS suits who insisted on putting him in stuff like this. How anyone could have gotten an idea of what the show was about from this promo is beyond me. I still don't know. Harry Morgan and Verna Felton were very talented but it seems like they're reduced to obvious physical humour and weak one-liners.
